newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Judge says IBM Argentina's ex-pres points to U.S..
newsitem.headline: Judge says IBM Argentina's ex-pres points to U.S..

text.p: An Argentine judge probing an alleged bribery case involving IBM's local unit said Thursday its imprisoned former president was insisting that the company's U.S. headquarters oversaw the deal under investigation.

Federal Judge Adolfo Bagnasco is investigating whether bribes were paid in 1993 to ensure that International Business Machines Corp won a contract to install a computer system for state-run Banco Nacion.
The judge told Reuters that former IBM Argentina President Ricardo Martorana argued he had "no operative responsibilities and no direct part in the contract with Banco Nacion."

Martorana added the $250 million deal in question was supervised by former IBM Argentina Vice President Gustavo Soriani, whose whereabouts are unknown to authorities, "and by IBM headquarters in the United States," Bagnasco said.
Martorana, who had also been at large, surrendered to Bagnasco this week. After an interrogation, the former IBM executive president was remanded in custody.
The judge in May had ordered the arrests of Martorana, Soriani, two former Banco Nacion officials and a former government official.
Bagnasco said he had just made his third request to U.S. authorities to send four U.S.-based IBM officials to Argentina to be questioned.

The four he summoned to testify on their alleged involvement in the scandal are Robeli Libero and Peter Rowley, former IBM Latin American president and Latin American vice president for marketing, respectively, and Marcio Kaiser and Steve Lew.

Bagnasco, who in the past threatened to ask Interpol to arrest the four if they did not come to Argentina, said he was repeating the summons because he had received no answer from U.S. courts. He has previously accused the U.S. courts of dragging their feet in the case.
At the heart of the probe are payments made to IBM's subcontractor CCR, which the judge suspects may have gone to alleged bribes for IBM Argentina to win the contract.
Bagnasco has asked U.S. authorities to provide him information on a Citicorp account in New York where money from CCR was transferred. He is also probing accounts in other banks.
He traced CCR's deposits worth about $9 million in an account of a Banque Bruxelles Lambert SA branch in Geneva, and at his request the Swiss supreme court lifted banking secrecy.
IBM Argentina has denied any wrongdoing although it has admitted to errors "inconsistent with company policy."
Other IBM Argentina deals are the subject of separate bribery probes.

One judge is investigating alleged "serious irregularities" in the $425 million deal between the unit and the country's tax collection body DGI, while another judge is probing why a contract between IBM Argentina and the Mendoza provincial government was awarded by decree instead of by public tender.
